requirements.requirement: On node1, root and opsadmin can schedule cron jobs, while users outside that allowlist cannot.
requirements.summary: The final policy contains exactly root and opsadmin, is root-owned with mode 0600, and direct tests before and after restart show both authorized users successfully installing crontabs while nobody receives an explicit denial. The Cronie service is enabled and running after restart.

overall_summary: The requested cron access control is satisfied. Exact allowlist inspection and behavioral tests demonstrate that root and opsadmin are permitted and an unlisted account is denied. The provider restart protocol is complete: healthy pre-restart state, restart acknowledgement, a changed boot identity corroborated by lifecycle observations, and recovered service, policy, accounts, and access behavior were all captured.
limitations: Only nobody was behaviorally tested as an unauthorized user; exclusivity for all other users is supported by the exact two-entry cron.allow policy.
The lifecycle collector cannot report failed OpenRC services because its failed-service probe is systemd-specific and unsupported on this node.
The evidence does not explain the precise semantics or originating command for the new `X etc/crontabs/root` package-health entry.

operational_hygiene.summary: The implementation succeeded, but there were three hygiene issues. The executor initially enabled the incompatible legacy crond OpenRC definition after installing Cronie; this was a low-risk unnecessary mutation that was fully reverted when the native cronie service replaced it. The reboot command left /tmp/benchmark-reboot.log behind. A new package-health discrepancy, `X etc/crontabs/root`, also remained after execution; temporary root-crontab tests were removed, but the evidence does not establish the exact cause or meaning of this discrepancy.
